title: Harness Relay: any mix of Claude Code, Codex, Grok and nine more coding agents
excerpt: The coding agents you already have, any mix of Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Cursor, Antigravity, Copilot, Muse Code and five open-source coding agents on your API keys or your own model, work with you and with each other. One kind is enough for a team. Design it, choose how they take turns, approve what they do.
content_html:
The coding agents you already have, working together

One kind of agent is enough for a team: all of one kind, or any mix of Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Cursor Agent, Antigravity, GitHub Copilot CLI, Muse Code and five open-source coding agents on your own model backends. For each question, the lead agent designs the team with each model’s own traits in mind: each member’s role and model, and how they take turns. Once you confirm it, the real agents on your machine work on your code, or any question, and answer each other.

Try it in Codespaces View on GitHub

Watch one run

A new group, then two questions on this repository, each with the team the lead agent chose for it, from the question to the answers, the code they discussed and a search. Sped up while the agents work.

The agents you installed, as they are

Harness Relay never calls a model API. It starts the claude, codex, grok, cursor-agent, agy, copilot and muse you already have, with their own tools, sessions and logins, passes each agent the messages it hasn’t seen yet, and streams everything into one conversation. OpenCode, Goose, Cline, OpenHands and Pi are started the same way, on the model backends you set up.

Claude Code
claude with stream-json in both directions; its permission requests become approval cards.

Codex
codex app-server: threads, turns and approval requests.

Grok
The Agent Client Protocol, over grok agent stdio.

Cursor
The Agent Client Protocol, over cursor-agent acp. It has no sandbox there, so below full access every command it wants to run asks you first (or is refused, if the conversation refuses automatically), except those on your Cursor team’s allowlist.

Antigravity
The Agent Client Protocol, over agy acp. It has no sandbox there either, so below full access every command it wants to run asks you first (or is refused, if the conversation refuses automatically), and a refusal ends its turn.

Copilot
The Agent Client Protocol, over copilot --acp. Below full access its commands run in Copilot’s own OS sandbox, whose policy Harness Relay checks before each turn, and a refusal ends its turn.

Muse Code
The Agent Client Protocol, over muse acp. Below full access its commands run in Muse Code’s own OS sandbox, which lets them write only in the working directories and the temp folder. In read-only every command asks you first; in edit mode, one that pushes or publishes; in both, one that wants the network.

One is enough, and any mix of the twelve works: the lead agent builds each team only from the agents you have ready, and several members can be the same agent, each with a role of its own. Sign in to Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Cursor, Antigravity, Copilot and Muse Code from Settings, and give the others a model backend.

Open-source agents, on your own model

OpenCode, Goose, Cline, OpenHands and Pi join a team like the other seven. They run on the model backends you set up in Settings: an API key for OpenAI, Anthropic or xAI, or your own OpenAI-compatible endpoint, such as vLLM, Ollama, LM Studio or llama.cpp.

OpenCode
opencode acp, the Agent Client Protocol.

Goose
goose acp, the Agent Client Protocol.

Cline
cline --acp, the Agent Client Protocol.

OpenHands
openhands acp, the Agent Client Protocol.

Pi
pi --mode rpc, JSONL RPC; below full access, a gate extension asks before each tool call.

Below full access, each of them, with everything it starts, runs in Harness Relay’s own OS sandbox. It writes only its own temp folder and its own sessions, which no other conversation’s agent can read or change, and in edit mode the working directory and the conversation’s attachments too. It reaches the run’s model backend without asking; other hosts are asked about, except this computer’s own addresses, a few the agent contacts by itself and any past the 30th in a run, which are refused. Approvals come as the same cards in the conversation.

Model backends

API keys

OpenAI · Set: ••••3f9a SaveRemove

Anthropic · Not set Save

xAI · Set: ••••7c21 SaveRemove

Custom endpoints

Homelab vLLM homelab/… http://10.0.0.5:8000/v1 · muse-glimmer-30b-nvfp4 EditDelete

＋ Add endpoint

Your keys, or your own endpoint

Give a member its model as backend/model: openai/gpt-5.4-nano, or your endpoint’s id and a model name, such as homelab/muse-glimmer-30b-nvfp4. Keys go to your OS credential store, and each run gets only its own backend’s key.

These agents take API keys only: the Claude subscription and Grok’s sign-in cannot be used by them. Claude Code and Grok themselves keep using their own sign-ins.

Interface excerpt recreated from the app, with sample content.

Choose how they take turns

Each conversation has its own rules: who speaks, in what order, and when it ends. Address anyone with an @mention and only they reply.

Roundtable

Agents speak in order, and each sees what earlier speakers said. Set one to five rounds; the run ends early when everyone in a round replies [PASS].

Good for discussions, reviews and refining an answer.

Parallel

Everyone answers at the same time, on their own. Later rounds see the earlier answers. With edit access each agent works in its own git worktree, and you apply the result you like.

Good for comparing approaches and getting independent opinions.

Relay

One agent at a time. An agent hands the floor to a teammate by @mentioning them; if it mentions nobody, the floor returns to you. You set the maximum number of hand-offs.

Good for pipelines: plan, implement, review.

A team for every question

The lead agent picks it. For each new question, it reads the question, the conversation so far, the current team and every template in full. Then it keeps the team, uses a template as it is, adapts one, or designs a new team, and says why. You confirm before the team answers, or let it answer right away.

It writes each role for its model. Claude, GPT, Gemini, Grok, Meta's Muse, Cursor's Composer and open-weight models each take instructions their own way, as their makers' own guides say. The lead agent writes each member's role the way that member's model takes it best, and reads only the guides for the models your agents run.

You design the templates. Give each agent a position (architect, builder, reviewer, skeptic), pick its model and reasoning effort, and set the speaking order. Up to eight members, several of them the same agent if you like. A team the lead agent designed can be kept as a template in one click.

Built-in templates

Auto team You confirm first

For each question, the lead agent picks a template, adapts one, or designs the team.

Architect → Builder → Reviewer Relay

Claude plans, Codex builds, Grok reviews, handing off with @mentions.

Three-way debate Roundtable × 2

Propose, challenge, converge. Good for technology choices and design discussions.

Parallel comparison Parallel

Three agents solve the same problem independently at the same time, for easy comparison.

General-question panel Roundtable

Not just code: analyse, fact-check and combine into one clear answer.

Pair programming + QA Roundtable

The Navigator directs, the Driver writes the code, QA writes tests and verifies.

You stay in charge

Agents work with the permission you choose for the conversation. Anything beyond it, they ask you there and wait.

@Adversarial_Reviewer Grok Round 2

@Adversarial_Reviewer wants to run a commandWaiting for you

npx tsx -e "import { mentionsInMarkdown } from './src/shared/mentions.ts'; …"

AllowAlways allow “npx tsx” in this chatDecline

Approvals in the conversation

Allow once, always allow it in this conversation, or decline with a note on what to do instead.

@Architect Claude Code

Before I compare the options: does the old /v1 API have to keep working, or may it break?

Waiting for your answer

Agents ask before guessing

When a good answer depends on something only you know, an agent asks and the team waits. Once you reply, that agent answers first, with your answer in hand.

@Builder Codex in worktree

  • Msrc/server/orchestrator.ts+42 −7
  • Msrc/server/prompt.ts+12 −3
  • Atest/relay.test.ts+88

View this turn’s diffApply to working directory

Every edit is a diff

The working directory becomes a git repository, and each reply lists the files that agent changed. In parallel mode every agent has its own worktree until you apply one result.

Also check what happens when an agent mentions nobody. EditWithdraw

Add to the discussion…Stop

Keep talking while they reply

A message sent mid-reply waits above the box and reaches the next agent before its turn. Edit or withdraw it until then, or stop the team and send it now.

Interface excerpts recreated from the app, with sample content.

Also in every conversation

  • Attach filesPaste screenshots or drop files. Every agent gets each file’s path, and the agents that take images see them directly.
  • Voice input, on your computerwhisper.cpp turns speech into text locally. Nothing is installed until you ask for it.
  • See what they think and doReasoning, plans and each tool’s output stream in. Mermaid blocks are drawn as diagrams.
  • Copy, edit and retryCopy a message or the whole conversation as Markdown. Edit your message or retry a reply, and the team answers again from there.
  • Branch a conversationBranch conversation, under a reply, copies the conversation up to that reply into a new one, to try another direction while the original stays as it was.
  • Share a conversation as a linkShare the whole conversation, or everything up to one reply, as a page that looks like the conversation on screen, without tool calls and thinking. It goes up as a secret gist with your GitHub CLI and opens on gistpreview.github.io; Settings lists every link, to remove the ones that should go.
  • Messages on a scheduleSend the team a message at set times, in the same conversation or in a new one each time: once, every day, every week on the days you pick, or every few hours. Or start from New schedule, and the lead agent picks the team. Nobody may be watching, so by default anything beyond the permission is refused automatically, unless you always allow it in that conversation. A time missed while Harness Relay was closed is skipped or, if you choose, sent once when it starts.
  • Status at a glanceThe sidebar marks conversations that need you, are replying or have a new reply. Conversations keep running when you switch away.
  • Notifications and soundWhen a reply is done or an agent needs you, a system notification and a short sound, turned on for each browser in Settings. On a phone with Harness Relay on its home screen, push notifications arrive even with the app closed or the phone locked.
  • Sign in from the appDevice-code, browser and paste-code sign-in for Claude Code, Codex, Grok, Cursor, Antigravity, Copilot and Muse Code, model backends for the open-source agents, plus API keys, executable paths and default models. See the skills, MCP tools, built-in tools, hooks, subagents, plugins, instructions and memory each agent loads by itself, and leave them out of Harness Relay's runs, all of a kind or one by one (Cursor and Antigravity have no way to, Muse Code only for its MCP servers and hooks).
  • Images and video in the conversationImages and videos an agent saves in the working directory show up right in the conversation.
  • Browse the working directoryFiles in the header lists the working directory, or an agent’s worktree, and previews code with line numbers, Markdown, images and video. Download any file, or a folder as a ZIP file.
  • One tool library for every memberMCP servers, skills and memory set up once reach every member, whichever of the twelve agents it is, on top of each agent’s own setup. Give each to some agents or to single members.
  • Every session in AgentsViewOptionally give the agents a folder of their own, and see each conversation in AgentsView as one thread, with every agent’s own session (tool calls, tokens and cost) under it, on all twelve agents (for Cursor and the open-source agents, the session Harness Relay recorded; Copilot’s without token counts on Windows).
  • English and 繁體中文The interface follows your browser’s language, with a guided tour on the first visit.

Runs on your machine

Harness Relay hosts nothing. The server listens on your computer only (when you try it in GitHub Codespaces, on your own codespace, at an address only your GitHub account can open), and agent replies cannot make your browser load remote content.

  • Bound to 127.0.0.1 and takes only browsers you signed in; cross-site requests are rejected.
  • Below full access, Claude Code’s, Codex’s, Grok’s, Copilot and Muse Code’s commands run in their own OS sandbox: they write only in the working directory, and can’t read your browsers’ folders or Harness Relay’s data. Cursor has no sandbox, so it asks you before every command (or refuses it, if the conversation refuses automatically), except those on your Cursor team’s allowlist. Antigravity has none either: it asks you before every command, and a refusal ends its turn. A refusal ends Copilot’s turn too.
  • The five open-source agents, and everything they start, run in Harness Relay’s own sandbox (sandbox-runtime: Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap on Linux, a filtering proxy for the network): the same folders are out of reach, each member’s sessions are its own, and only the run’s model backend is reachable without asking. If it can’t start, they don’t run; on native Windows they run only with full access.
  • Git snapshots for every turn that edits; parallel agents in their own worktrees.
  • API keys and MCP server tokens in your OS credential store: macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager or Secret Service; where there is none, as in a codespace, encrypted in the database.
  • Your conversations live in one SQLite file; Harness Relay publishes one only when you share it as a link.
File permission, set per conversation
Read-only Reading, searching and looking things up on the web.
Edit Also editing files in the working directory and running project commands such as tests and builds. Pushing and publishing are not included.
Full access Everything, without asking. Use it only in directories you trust.

In edit mode, tests and scripts run code the agents can change. Codex’s sandbox keeps it off the network; Claude Code’s, and Harness Relay’s own around the open-source agents, ask you about each host (an open agent reaches its model backend without asking), and Muse Code’s before a command reaches the network; Grok’s and Copilot’s commands can still reach the network, and Cursor and Antigravity have no sandbox (a command you allow runs with your rights). On native Windows only Codex , Copilot and Muse Code have a sandbox (Muse Code’s after its own one-time setup, which asks for administrator rights; until then its commands fail). For code or instructions you don’t trust, use read-only. What each sandbox covers, by platform

Quick start

  1. Install one agent or more

    • Any of these agents: Claude Code (claude), Codex CLI (codex), Grok CLI (grok), Cursor CLI (cursor-agent), Antigravity CLI (agy), GitHub Copilot CLI (copilot), Muse Code (muse)
    • Or the open-source ones (versions tested): OpenCode (opencode-ai 1.19.5), Goose (block-goose-cli 1.58.1), Cline (cline 3.0.74), OpenHands (openhands 1.16.0), Pi (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent 1.5.1, Node.js 22.19 or newer), with an API key for OpenAI, Anthropic or xAI, or your own endpoint. Below full access they run in a sandbox that needs Node.js 22.12 or newer, and on Linux also bubblewrap, socat and ripgrep.
    • Git, for edit and parallel modes. Nothing else: the app brings what it runs on

  2. Download and open it

    macOSmacOS 13 or later · Apple Silicon · .dmg Your system WindowsWindows 10 or later, x64 · .exe Your system Windows on ArmWindows 10 or later, Arm64 · .exe Your system Linuxx64 · .AppImage Your system Linux on ArmArm64 (aarch64) · .AppImage Your system

    All installers are on the releases page.

    On macOS, drag Harness Relay to Applications; on Windows, the installer sets it up for your user; on Linux, make the AppImage executable and run it. The installers are not signed yet, so the first time: on macOS, System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway; on Windows, More info → Run anyway.

  3. Sign in, then get to work

    Harness Relay opens in a window of its own, signed in, and stays in the menu bar (or the system tray) when you close it, so your phone can still reach it. Under Settings & sign-in, check that each agent is signed in, or, for the open-source agents, add an API key or your endpoint under Model backends. Then New chat: choose the working directory and permission, and ask your first question.

  4. Open it on your phone

    Optional. Install Tailscale on the computer and on the phone, then choose Share with your phone (Tailscale)… in Harness Relay's menu. It shares the server with your tailnet and shows the https:// address to open on the phone.

    Sign the phone in with a code from Settings → Signed-in browsers → Sign in another device on the computer. Only devices in your tailnet can reach it, and the server stays on 127.0.0.1. To add it to the home screen: Share → Add to Home Screen in Safari on iPhone, ⋮ → Install app in Chrome on Android. Then turn on Settings → Notifications and sound there, to be told when the team finishes or needs you, even with the phone locked.

    Step by step, with keeping it running and troubleshooting

Codex’s sandbox keeps it off the network; Claude Code’s, and Harness Relay’s own around the open-source agents, ask you about each host (an open agent reaches its model backend without asking), and Muse Code’s before a command reaches the network; Grok’s and Copilot’s commands can still reach the network, and Cursor and Antigravity have no sandbox (a command you allow runs with your rights). On native Windows only Codex , Copilot and Muse Code have a sandbox (Muse Code’s after its own one-time setup, which asks for administrator rights; until then its commands fail). For code or instructions you don’t trust, use read-only. On macOS, drag Harness Relay to Applications; on Windows, the installer sets it up for your user; on Linux, make the AppImage executable and run it. The installers are not signed yet, so the first time: on macOS, System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway; on Windows, More info → Run anyway. Sign in, then get to work Harness Relay opens in a window of its own, signed in, and stays in the menu bar (or the system tray) when you close it, so your phone can still reach it. Under Settings & sign-in, check that each agent is signed in, or, for the open-source agents, add an API key or your endpoint under Model backends. Then New chat: choose the working directory and permission, and ask your first question. Open it on your phone Optional. Install Tailscale on the computer and on the phone, then choose Share with your phone (Tailscale)… in Harness Relay's menu. It shares the server with your tailnet and shows the https:// address to open on the phone. Sign the phone in with a code from Settings → Signed-in browsers → Sign in another device on the computer. Only devices in your tailnet can reach it, and the server stays on 127.0.0.1. To add it to the home screen: Share → Add to Home Screen in Safari on iPhone, ⋮ → Install app in Chrome on Android.
